ov: A short, lyrical novel narrated by the Roman poet Ovid, banished by Augustus to the edge of the known world. Stripped of his language, status and audience, he finds a new way of seeing the world through a wild child who lives among wolves. In the Common Module, it tests what we assume about human strength (reputation, civilisation, mastery of words) and shows how vulnerability can become the beginning of growth and belonging.
rub: Language, forms and features: first-person lyrical prose, the present tense, dreams, the cyclical structure and sensory description shape meaning.
Identity, culture, acceptance and growth: Ovid is remade through exile and through the Child.
Challenging assumptions: civilisation versus the wild, speech versus silence, age versus youth.
sum: Ovid, the celebrated Roman poet, has been exiled to Tomis, a remote settlement on the Black Sea. He is old, isolated and hears no word of his own language; he must relearn the world through the speech of his hosts. He remembers a boyhood companion, the Child, an image of a wild boy who lived with wolves. When villagers on a hunting trip glimpse a wild child in the forest, Ovid becomes obsessed with finding him. The Child is eventually taken, and Ovid tries to teach him language, tools and human habits, while the Child begins to teach Ovid how to belong to the earth. When winter and the community’s fears close in, Ovid and the Child leave on a journey into the wilderness. Ovid’s old self falls away, and the novel closes in a vision that collapses time: “I am three years old. I am sixty. I am six. I am there.”
acts: Ovid recalls a childhood friend he called the Child, an invisible companion, and hears of a wild boy among wolves.
Isolated and speechless, Ovid struggles to survive among the villagers. He relearns the world word by word, noticing a poppy as if for the first time.
Ovid joins the villagers on a hunting trip into the forest. He sets out food for the Child and dreams of becoming part of the woods.
The Child is brought into Tomis. Ovid teaches him words, and the Child’s presence changes Ovid’s idea of language and of himself.
The two leave the settlement. Ovid’s body and past drop away as he moves toward the Child’s world.
Time collapses into a single moment of childhood and age, ending with Ovid’s sense that “I am there.”
ch: Once admired and worldly, he becomes humble and receptive. His arc moves from self-pity to wonder to acceptance.
I am the least person here – a crazy, comic old man, grotesque, tearful, who understands nothing.
Wild boy who lives among wolves
A figure of instinct, silence and possibility. He is both a real child and a symbol of the unspoilt self.
Practical, gruff and embarrassed by Ovid’s obsession. He represents the community’s fear of the wild.
He thinks this is all folly. And dangerous folly.
The power that has silenced Ovid, a symbol of empire, order and control.
Of course in the short run Augustus wins.
cx: David Malouf (born Brisbane, 1934) wrote this novel in the 1970s. In the author’s note he explains that his wild child is partly drawn from J.M.G. Itard’s observations of Victor, the wild boy of Aveyron, and that he set the story in a remote place about which almost nothing is known so that the narrative could move in more open possibilities.

Ovid (43 BCE–c. 17 CE) was the Roman poet of the Metamorphoses (“the changes”). Malouf makes this “glib fabulist” live out transformation in reality. The novel plays with the contrast between Roman civilisation and the so-called barbarian world, and invites readers to question which is more human.

Augustus banished Ovid to Tomis on the Black Sea in 8 CE for reasons never fully explained. The Roman Empire is shown as sophisticated but controlling. Malouf notes that the actual date and cause of Ovid’s death remain mysterious, which gave him freedom to imagine.

Themes of exile, language loss and the relationship between civilisation and nature resonate with Australian questions about place, belonging and migration, and with the Enlightenment debate over nature and nurture.
im: Wolves and the forest: they appear in Ovid’s first memory and in his later dreams. They represent the wild that civilisation fears and that Ovid comes to embrace.
The scarlet poppy: the first colour Ovid has seen in months. The word and the flower revive his senses and show the power of naming.
Snow and the frozen river: winter closes the settlement and tests endurance; the river is a threshold between worlds.
The pool in Ovid’s dream: “I am a pool of water”, an image of dissolving into nature and being drunk from by a deer.
th: Words create and limit our world. Ovid’s loss of language humbles him; the Child’s learning of words transforms them both.
Common Module: the power of language to express personal ideas and experience.
Exile strips Ovid of status and makes him vulnerable; belonging is found in nature, not in empire.

Ovid’s strength lies in his capacity to be remade.

The wild is not the enemy of the human but the origin of it.

A.i: David Malouf’s An Imaginary Life offers readers the opportunity to examine assumptions about human strength and vulnerability by placing the celebrated poet Ovid in exile, where the traditional markers of strength (status, language, reputation) are stripped away. Through Ovid’s humiliation and his bond with the wild Child, Malouf suggests that vulnerability is not the opposite of strength but its source. The novel’s lyrical, first-person voice invites audiences to see human endurance as an openness to being remade.
b: Malouf first dismantles the assumption that strength lies in status. Ovid confesses that he is “the least person here – a crazy, comic old man, grotesque, tearful, who understands nothing.” The asyndetic list of harsh adjectives and the self-mockery strip away the poet’s pride and expose him as others see him. His loss of language intensifies this vulnerability: “for nearly a year now I have heard no word of my own language; I am rendered dumb.” The passive voice casts Ovid as acted upon, and the blunt statement of silence removes the poet’s greatest power. Strength, by the usual measures, has gone.

From this humiliation, Malouf reveals a different kind of strength: the willingness to learn. Ovid asks, “Will I have to learn everything all over again like a child?”, and the rhetorical question shifts his fear towards curiosity. The sensory epiphany that follows, “Scarlet! It is the first color I have seen in months”, uses exclamation to enact a sudden rebirth, and he adds that “the saying [is] almost a greater miracle than the seeing.” Vulnerability here is the condition for wonder. By reducing Ovid to a child, the text challenges the assumption that maturity and mastery are the same as strength.

Finally, Malouf suggests that strength is found in surrender to something larger. Ovid dreams that “we have all been transformed, the whole group of us, and become part of the woods”, an image of metamorphosis that dissolves the boundary between self and nature. The novel closes with the paradoxical “I am three years old. I am sixty. I am six. I am there.” The anaphora and the collapsing of time create a moment of transcendence, where the old poet’s weakness becomes a joyful union with the Child. Endurance is no longer survival but belonging.
A.c: Ultimately, Malouf invites audiences to reconsider the relationship between strength and vulnerability. Ovid’s power to remain open to change, rather than to command, is the novel’s truest strength, and his final transformation suggests that being undone can be the beginning of being whole.
A.n: What to notice: a thesis that defines strength in a new way (“vulnerability is the source of strength”). Each paragraph has a clear idea, uses three pieces of evidence, names techniques (asyndeton, passive voice, rhetorical question, anaphora) and explains the effect. Language from the question and module (assumptions, strength and vulnerability, growth) is used throughout.

B.i: In An Imaginary Life, David Malouf shows how strength and vulnerability are connected. Through the poet Ovid, who is exiled to a remote land, the novel challenges our ideas about what it means to be strong.
b: At first, Ovid is weak. He says he is “the least person here – a crazy, comic old man.” This shows he feels worthless. He also says, “I am rendered dumb”, because he cannot speak the language. This shows that exile has taken away his power as a poet. The list of words shows how low he feels.

Ovid then becomes stronger when he learns. He asks, “Will I have to learn everything all over again like a child?” and he is amazed by a red flower: “Scarlet!” The exclamation shows his joy. This shows that Ovid is strong because he is willing to start again.

At the end, Ovid dreams that “we have all been transformed”, which shows that he feels part of nature. The last lines, “I am three years old. I am sixty. I am six. I am there”, show that Ovid is happy and that he has found a connection with the Child.
B.c: In conclusion, Malouf shows that vulnerability can lead to strength. Ovid starts as a lonely exile but ends up happy.
B.n: What to notice: a clear argument and relevant quotes, but the analysis stays general (“this shows that…”). Techniques are named only occasionally, the effects are not explained, and the question’s key word “assumptions” is not addressed.

models.C: In An Imaginary Life Ovid is exiled and cannot speak the language. This makes him vulnerable. He finds a child and teaches him words. The author uses a first person narrator. This shows strength and vulnerability.
models.D: An Imaginary Life is about a man called Ovid who goes away and meets a child. He is sad and then he is happy.

A.i: Through the particular lives of the exiled poet Ovid and the wild Child, David Malouf’s An Imaginary Life enriches our understanding of the endurance of the human spirit as an imaginative, rather than merely physical, power. Written in Ovid’s present-tense voice, the novel shows a life stripped of status and language, yet endlessly capable of wonder. In doing so, it invites audiences to see endurance as the capacity to keep naming, dreaming and transforming.
b: Malouf represents Ovid’s life as an act of endurance through language. Isolated in Tomis, he says, “In the open I go about shouting, talking to myself simply to keep the words in my head”, and the image of a man shouting to the empty air dramatises the spirit’s refusal to be silenced. When he sees a poppy, “Scarlet! It is the first color I have seen in months”, the exclamation and the repeated word show how naming can rescue the senses. His voice is therefore the particular life that enriches our understanding: endurance here is the stubborn need to speak.

The Child’s life offers a contrasting kind of endurance. “He is a wild boy”, the blunt statement, locates him outside human language and civilisation, while the repeated “The child is always the same age” makes him timeless. His survival among wolves suggests that the spirit persists without the supports of empire or speech. As Ovid teaches him words and the Child teaches Ovid to belong to the earth, Malouf shows that endurance is reciprocal: two lives, one old and one wild, sustain each other.

Finally, Malouf’s closing vision suggests that the human spirit endures by transcending time. Ovid’s dream that “we have all been transformed… and become part of the woods” prepares for the final paradox, “I am three years old. I am sixty. I am six. I am there.” The anaphora of “I am” and the collapse of time unite age and childhood in a single moment of joy. These particular lives show that the spirit endures not by conquering circumstance but by being absorbed into something larger.
A.c: Malouf’s representation of Ovid and the Child therefore deepens our understanding of endurance as imaginative, reciprocal and transcendent. Their particular lives remind us that the human spirit survives wherever there is language, wonder and a willingness to be changed.
A.n: What to notice: the thesis defines endurance (imaginative power) and ties it to “particular lives” (Ovid and the Child). The paragraphs follow the argument from exile to reciprocity to transcendence, and quotes are used with technique and effect each time.

B.i: In An Imaginary Life, David Malouf shows the endurance of the human spirit through the life of Ovid and the Child. They both survive difficulties and find hope.
b: Ovid shows endurance when he is alone in exile. He says, “In the open I go about shouting, talking to myself simply to keep the words in my head.” This shows he is trying to hold on to language. When he sees a red flower, he says, “Scarlet!”, which shows that he is excited and alive again.

The Child also shows endurance. He lives with wolves, and Malouf says, “He is a wild boy.” This shows that he can survive without help. Ovid teaches the Child words and the Child changes Ovid, which shows that they help each other.
At the end Ovid says, “I am three years old. I am sixty. I am six. I am there.” This shows that he has found happiness and that his spirit survives.
B.c: In conclusion, Malouf shows endurance through the lives of Ovid and the Child. They overcome challenges and find peace.
B.n: What to notice: relevant quotes and a clear argument, but the evidence is stated rather than analysed. There is little discussion of technique, and “enriches our understanding” is not explicitly addressed.
